questions.question: A team's position reads: "The AI-powered workspace for modern teams." What single test shows it is not yet strategic?
options: It does not mention a measurable outcome for the customer
No real customer request is declined by it
It does not name the technology that powers the AI layer
It was written by product rather than by marketing
questions.explanation: Information in a position comes from what it rules out, so the test is whether anything gets declined. A is the competent-sounding distractor: adding an outcome metric makes the sentence more specific without making it exclude anyone, so the same requests still qualify.

questions.question: Noted's PM claims the sustaining capability for a small-team position is its team collaboration environment. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Collaboration environments are commodity features and cannot ever be an advantage
Small teams have not requested collaboration features loudly enough to justify it
That environment is in design, not live, so the position is currently undefended
The capability belongs to engineering, so product cannot claim it
questions.explanation: The case separates live, in design, and planned, and a capability that is in design is an intention. Betting on it can be legitimate, but it must be labelled a bet. A is tempting because it sounds hard-headed, but it is an unsupported general rule; the actual defect here is the status of the capability, not its category.

questions.question: A PM decides to position around small teams and give up enterprise team leads. The account manager asks whether existing enterprise contracts must be dropped. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes — serving them contradicts the position and will erode focus
No — giving up an audience means they stop shaping direction, not that their money is refused
Yes, but only after the contracts reach their renewal dates
No — the position applies to new customers only, so nothing changes
questions.explanation: Sacrifice is about who has a claim on your roadmap and your default experience, not about revenue you already hold. D is the tempting distractor because it sounds pragmatic, but it makes the position apply to nobody who currently generates pressure, which removes the sacrifice entirely.

questions.question: Which of these differences is closest to a genuine advantage?
options: A faster editor built on a recently released open-source component
A more attractive empty-state design that tests well with new users
A broader feature set than the two nearest competitors
A retrieval quality benefit that comes from years of accumulated in-product usage data
questions.explanation: It is valued, it rests on an asset that takes time to accumulate, and a competitor cannot buy the history. C is the tempting answer: breadth feels like strength, but it is copyable, expensive to hold, and usually the result of having declined nothing.

questions.question: A seed-stage team cannot yet tell which of two audiences it serves. What does the boundary of this model permit?
options: Holding both audiences indefinitely, since focus destroys early learning
Choosing the audience with the larger addressable market and committing now
Holding both with a stated resource split and a date at which one is dropped
Positioning against the alternative rather than the audience until this is resolved
questions.explanation: Holding two candidates while testing is honest when it is time-boxed and the split is visible. A is the tempting version of the same idea, and it is where most teams end up: without a date, learning becomes the permanent excuse for never choosing.
